findings.title: Server-Side JavaScript injection via eval() of contribution inputs
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user POSTs to /contributions with preTax set to a JavaScript expression (e.g. a process-spawning or infinite-loop payload). handleContributionsUpdate calls eval(req.body.preTax) directly, executing attacker code in the Node.js process before the numeric validation runs, yielding remote code execution and a pivot point into the host and MongoDB.
findings.remediation: Replace eval() with parseInt()/Number() parsing and reject non-numeric input (the commented-out fix in contributions.js). Never evaluate request bodies.

findings.title: NoSQL ($where) injection via allocations stocks threshold
findings.attack_path: Attacker passes ?threshold=0';while(true){}' (or '; return 1=='1) to GET /allocations/:userId. getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the raw threshold into a {$where: "... this.stocks > '<threshold>'"} clause that MongoDB executes as server-side JavaScript, enabling data exfiltration across all users and a server-side JS DoS.
findings.remediation: Eliminate $where; coerce threshold with parseInt and bound 0-99, then use a typed comparison query ({stocks:{$gt:n}}). Apply the commented-out validation in allocations-dao.js.

findings.title: Cleartext password storage and plaintext credential comparison
findings.attack_path: addUser stores the raw password field with no hashing; validateLogin compares fromDB === fromUser in plaintext. Any read of the users collection (via NoSQL injection TM-002/TM-018, a Mongo compromise TM-021, or a backup leak) exposes every credential directly, enabling immediate account takeover and credential reuse against other systems.
findings.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync on signup, bcrypt.compareSync on login) per the commented fix; never store or compare plaintext.

findings.title: Stored XSS via shared memo board with template autoescape disabled
findings.attack_path: A user POSTs a memo containing <script> to /memos. MemosDAO stores it verbatim and getAllMemos returns it to EVERY user (the board is global). Swig is configured autoescape:false in server.js, so the payload renders unescaped in every viewer's session, including any admin who opens /memos, stealing session cookies (httpOnly is not set) and chaining to admin account takeover.
findings.remediation: Enable swig autoescape:true, contextually output-encode memo content, and scope memos per user. Set cookie httpOnly/secure flags.

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on /allocations/:userId
findings.attack_path: displayAllocations reads userId from the URL params, not the session. Because user IDs are small sequential integers from the counters collection, any authenticated user iterates /allocations/1, /allocations/2, ... to read every other user's portfolio and name, with no ownership check.
findings.remediation: Derive userId from req.session (the commented fix) and never trust the path parameter for authorization.

findings.title: Missing function-level access control on /benefits (admin function exposed to all users)
findings.attack_path: An isAdmin middleware exists but the /benefits GET/POST routes only apply isLoggedIn. Any authenticated non-admin can load the benefits admin screen and POST arbitrary benefitStartDate values for any user, an unauthorized privileged business function and a vertical-privilege gap across trust boundary TB3.
findings.remediation: Add isAdmin to both /benefits routes (the commented fix in index.js) and enforce role checks server-side on every privileged action.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via /research url parameter
findings.attack_path: displayResearch builds url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol and passes it straight to needle.get, returning the response body to the client. An authenticated attacker points url at http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata) or internal services to read instance credentials and pivot, with the fetched body reflected back unescaped.
findings.remediation: Remove user control of the base URL; allow only an allow-listed stock-data host, validate scheme/host, and block link-local/internal ranges.

findings.title: NoSQL operator-injection authentication bypass on /login
findings.attack_path: bodyParser.json() is enabled, so a JSON login body {"userName":{"$gt":""},"password":{"$gt":""}} reaches usersCol.findOne({userName}) untyped. The operator object matches the first user (admin), and because the password is then compared in plaintext the attacker controls comparison semantics, enabling authentication bypass without credentials.
findings.remediation: Coerce userName/password to strings before querying, reject non-string login fields, and use a constant-time hashed comparison.

findings.title: No transport encryption (cleartext HTTP) with committed TLS private key
findings.attack_path: server.js serves over plain http.createServer (the https block is commented out), so credentials, session cookies, SSN and bank data cross TB1 in cleartext and are interceptable by any network MITM. Worse, the matching private key artifacts/cert/server.key is committed to the repo, so even if TLS were enabled it provides no confidentiality.
findings.remediation: Terminate TLS (enable the https server), set Strict-Transport-Security, and rotate then remove the committed key/cert from version control.

findings.title: Sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, bank account/routing) stored unencrypted
findings.attack_path: ProfileDAO.updateUser writes ssn, dob, bankAcc, bankRouting as plaintext fields on the user document (the encryption helpers are commented out). Any data-store read primitive (TM-002, TM-008, TM-021) or backup exposure leaks regulated financial PII for all users, a reportable breach.
findings.remediation: Encrypt SSN/DOB/bank fields at rest (the commented crypto helpers, with a proper random IV and KMS-managed key) and minimize what is collected.

findings.title: Default/seed accounts with weak, well-known credentials
findings.attack_path: artifacts/db-reset.js seeds admin/Admin_123 (isAdmin:true) plus user1/User1_123 and user2/User2_123. These predictable credentials are public in the repo and run via the Heroku postdeploy and docker-compose startup, so any deployment ships with a guessable admin login.
findings.remediation: Remove default-credential seeding from any non-local environment; require an out-of-band admin bootstrap with a randomly generated password.

findings.title: Hardcoded application secrets (session cookie secret and crypto key) in source
findings.attack_path: config/env/all.js hardcodes cookieSecret = 'session_cookie_secret_key_here' and cryptoKey = 'a_secure_key_for_crypto_here'. Knowing the cookie secret lets an attacker forge/ tamper with signed session cookies and impersonate any user; the static crypto key undermines any at-rest encryption built on it.
findings.remediation: Load secrets from environment/secret manager, generate strong random values per deployment, and rotate the committed values.

findings.title: Session fixation and insecure session cookie configuration
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate(), so a session id fixed before login (over cleartext HTTP, TM-009) survives privilege elevation. Cookies lack httpOnly/secure/maxAge, and saveUninitialized:true with a default MemoryStore compounds fixation and theft.
findings.remediation: Regenerate the session id on login, set cookie httpOnly+secure+SameSite+maxAge, set saveUninitialized:false, and use a persistent server-side session store.

findings.title: No CSRF protection on state-changing POST endpoints
findings.attack_path: csurf is imported but commented out in server.js and the profile template emits an empty _csrf token. A logged-in victim who visits an attacker page is forced to POST /profile, /contributions, /benefits or /memos with attacker values (chaining to the eval RCE TM-001 or stored XSS TM-004).
findings.remediation: Enable csurf, expose the token to templates, and require it on every state-changing request; add SameSite cookies as defense in depth.

findings.title: Regular-expression denial of service in bank-routing validation
findings.attack_path: handleProfileUpdate validates bankRouting with /([0-9]+)+#/, a nested-quantifier pattern subject to catastrophic backtracking. A POST /profile with a long all-digit string and no # pins the single-threaded Node event loop at 100% CPU, denying service to all users.
findings.remediation: Replace with a linear pattern such as /([0-9]+)#/ (the commented fix) and add input length limits.

findings.title: Verbose error and stack-trace disclosure to clients
findings.attack_path: errorHandler renders the full error object into error-template.html ({{error}}) and logs the stack. Triggering an exception (e.g. malformed input, the $where DoS) returns internal paths, query structure, and stack frames to the attacker, aiding further exploitation.
findings.remediation: Return a generic error page to clients, log details server-side only, and never serialize the error object into the response.

findings.title: Log injection / CRLF log forging via login username
findings.attack_path: On a failed login the raw userName is written to console.log with no CRLF sanitization. An attacker submits a username containing newline sequences and forged log lines to corrupt audit logs, hide activity, or poison downstream log processors that trust the format.
findings.remediation: Strip/encode CR/LF in user input before logging (the commented ESAPI/replace fix) and use structured logging.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via profile website field encoded for wrong context
findings.attack_path: displayProfile HTML-encodes doc.website then the template uses it as an href (<a href="{{firstNameSafeString}}">) with autoescape off. HTML-context encoding does not neutralize a javascript: URI or attribute breakout, so a stored website value executes script when the profile is viewed.
findings.remediation: Encode for the URL/attribute context (ESAPI encodeForURL), validate the scheme is http/https, and enable template autoescaping.

findings.title: MongoDB reachable without authentication (implicit network trust)
findings.attack_path: The connection string mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat (config) and the docker-compose mongo service carry no credentials and the app trusts the DB purely by network position (TB4). An attacker who reaches the Mongo port, or who pivots via SSRF/RCE, reads and modifies every collection including plaintext passwords and PII with no further authentication.
findings.remediation: Enable MongoDB authentication and TLS, scope a least-privilege application user, and network-isolate the database; do not rely on localhost trust.

findings.title: Open redirect via /learn url parameter
findings.attack_path: GET /learn does res.redirect(req.query.url) with no validation. An attacker crafts a /learn?url=https://evil.example link that, once a victim is logged in, bounces them to a phishing site under the trusted application's domain, aiding credential theft.
findings.remediation: Redirect only to a server-side allow-list of relative paths/known hosts; reject absolute external URLs.

findings.title: Outdated and unmaintained dependencies with known weaknesses
findings.attack_path: package.json pins old releases: mongodb 2.x (server-side $where JS enabling TM-002), swig 1.4.2 (unmaintained, autoescape default off), marked 0.3.5, bcrypt-nodejs 0.0.3. A published CVE in any of these, delivered through the build pipeline (TB6), compromises the running app and its data.
findings.remediation: Upgrade to maintained versions, run npm audit / retire.js in CI as a gate, and pin via lockfile with periodic patching.

findings.title: Weak password policy at signup
findings.attack_path: validateSignup accepts any password matching /^.{1,20}$/ (a single character qualifies). Combined with no rate limiting on /login (TM-023) and plaintext storage (TM-003), trivial passwords make brute-force and credential-guessing attacks highly effective.
findings.remediation: Enforce the commented strong policy (min length, mixed case, digits), add login rate limiting/lockout, and screen against breached-password lists.

findings.title: Username enumeration and missing brute-force protection on login
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest returns distinct messages ('Invalid username' vs 'Invalid password'), letting an attacker enumerate valid accounts. There is no attempt throttling or lockout, so enumeration plus unlimited guessing against weak/plaintext passwords yields account takeover.
findings.remediation: Return one generic error for both cases (the commented fix), and add rate limiting, lockout, and CAPTCHA/throttling on repeated failures.

findings.title: Missing HTTP security headers (clickjacking, MIME sniffing, no HSTS/CSP)
findings.attack_path: All helmet middleware (frameguard, noCache, CSP, HSTS, noSniff) and x-powered-by removal are commented out in server.js. The app sends no X-Frame-Options/CSP, so it can be framed for clickjacking, has no MIME-sniffing protection, and advertises its stack, enabling UI-redress and content-injection attacks.
findings.remediation: Enable helmet with frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts, noSniff, and disable x-powered-by.

findings.title: Committed ZAP API key in committed environment config
findings.attack_path: config/env/development.js and config/env/test.js commit a static ZAP apiKey ('v9dn0balpqas1pcc281tn5ood1') and fixed scanner host/port. While scoped to test tooling, committing the key normalizes secret-in-repo practice and could expose a debugging ZAP instance if those configs are reused.
findings.remediation: Move scanner credentials to environment variables/secret store and rotate the committed key.

findings.title: Container/runtime hardening gaps in build and deploy pipeline
findings.attack_path: The Dockerfile leaves the production chown/chmod hardening line commented, the docker-compose web service runs without resource/permission limits, and CI starts the app with seeded default accounts. A compromise of an app dependency or the eval RCE (TM-001) inherits broad filesystem permissions and can persist in the image/build chain (TB6).
findings.remediation: Uncomment and apply the non-root hardening in the Dockerfile, drop container capabilities, set read-only filesystem where possible, and keep seed/default accounts out of any shared image.
